sources.title: How To Make Salt
sources.publisher: National Park Service (Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, 'Pivotal Places')
sources.supports: Field, Bratton and Gibson made salt near a Clatsop-Nehalem village on the Oregon coast in winter 1805-1806; equipment named (five kettles, wood, rocks, iron kegs, seawater); NPS says almost a gallon a day working around the clock; Lewis's 'very tedious opperation' and mid-February stock of about 20 gallons with 12 secured in two kegs; Clark's remark that the salt was not so strong as rock salt.
sources.notes: Interpretive article, not a research paper. NPS says 'almost a gallon of salt a day'; the journals say 3 quarts to a gallon a day (5 Jan 1806). Extent read: full page text (single short article), live scrape.

sources.title: Salt Works, Oregon
sources.publisher: National Park Service (Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail / Lewis and Clark National Historical Park)
sources.supports: The party ran out of salt and chose to winter near the ocean to make it; salt valued for preserving meat; the three salt makers befriended people of the Clatsop-Nehalem village, who sold them whale blubber; about twenty gallons made by Lewis's count; the site is a replica salt works in Seaside, Oregon.
sources.notes: NPS says Clark did not mind going without salt while Lewis found unsalted food bland; the journals confirm the contrast (5 Jan 1806). Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: December 28, 1805 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
sources.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
sources.supports: Clark's entry detailing Joseph Field, Bratton and Gibson to form a camp at the ocean and 'Commence makeing Salt with 5 of the largest Kittles', with Willard and Wiser carrying kettles; Ordway and Whitehouse entries; editorial note that the camp was at present Seaside, ran until 21 February 1806 and produced about three or four bushels; editorial note on Clatsop winter villages at Seaside.
sources.notes: The editors' footnote (three or four bushels) and the NPS gallon figures are different units and are not reconciled by any source we read. Extent read: the whole page (Clark x2, Ordway, Whitehouse entries and editors' footnotes 1-5), live scrape. No other journal dates were read except 5 Jan and 21 Feb 1806.

sources.title: January 5, 1806 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
sources.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
sources.supports: Lewis and Clark on the first salt delivered by Willard and Wiser: camp on the coast about 15 miles from the fort near Killamuck (Lewis) / Clat Sop and Kil a mox (Clark) families; salt makers got from 3 quarts to a gallon a day; a gallon specimen; Lewis 'excellent, fine, strong, & white'; Clark 'not So Strong as the rock Salt'; no salt since 20 December; whale blubber from the Indians; Ordway and Whitehouse accounts.
sources.notes: Lewis and Clark's descriptions of the salt differ in wording; Lewis names the neighbours Killamuck (Tillamook), Clark names Clatsop and Killamuck. Extent read: the whole page (Lewis, Clark, Ordway, Gass, Whitehouse entries and footnotes), live scrape.

sources.title: February 21, 1806 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
sources.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
sources.supports: The salt camp evacuated; the party returned with the salt and utensils; Lewis: stock of salt now about 20 gallons, 12 secured in 2 small iron-bound kegs for the voyage; Ordway's account of the wet return to the fort; Gass and Whitehouse accounts.
sources.notes: NPS and the Lewis journal agree on 20 and 12 gallons. The editors date the end of the camp 21 February; the 1955 plaque quoted by another site says 20 February. Extent read: the whole page (Lewis, Clark, Ordway, Gass, Whitehouse entries and footnotes), live scrape.

sources.title: The Salt Works (Discover Lewis & Clark)
sources.publisher: Lewis and Clark Trail Alliance
sources.supports: Secondary account of the salt works: why the camp was on the coast rather than the Netul River; five days to find a site; the oven reassembled as a 'cairn' in the 1950s; plaque text crediting the site to the testimony of Jenny Michel, whose Clatsop father pointed it out; the plaque's 'approximately four bushels' and end date.
sources.notes: Public-service educational site run by the Lewis and Clark Trail Alliance; kind 'nonprofit' is the closest fit (nonprofit status not confirmed from the page). Its figures of 28 gallons produced and about 1,400 gallons of seawater are not sourced on the page and are not used as fact in our article. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: History & Culture: People: Tribes (Lewis and Clark National Historical Park)
sources.publisher: National Park Service
sources.supports: The Clatsop lived on the south side of the Columbia and down the coast to Tillamook Head; the Nehalem are described as the northernmost band of the Tillamook, from Tillamook Head south to Kilchis Point; the Chinook lived on the north bank; the captains described friendly relations; Coboway received the fort; the page names the Clatsop-Nehalem Confederated Tribes and the Chinook Nation as homeland tribes.
sources.notes: Read through a search result excerpt that reproduced the full page text, then not re-fetched; flagged for a human link check. Extent read: the full page text as reproduced in a search-result excerpt; the live page was not separately scraped.

sources.title: Hardtack during the Civil War
sources.publisher: National Park Service, Manassas National Battlefield Park (youth page)
sources.supports: Civil War hardtack was made from flour, water and salt; soldiers' nicknames ('sheet iron crackers', 'tooth duller', 'worm castles'); it got wet and moldy in shipping boxes and could hold insect eggs; soldiers softened it in coffee, put it in soups, fried it; Confederates relied more on corn because wheat was less widely grown; hardtack from the war survives in the park museum.
sources.notes: A youth page. It includes a home recipe with quantities, which we deliberately do not reproduce or link. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: Cooking - Food Rations
sources.publisher: National Park Service, Fort Scott National Historic Site
sources.supports: U.S. Army daily ration of the 1840s (pork or salt beef, flour made into bread, beans or rice, coffee, sugar, vinegar, salt); hardtack issued on campaign and often in camp, about a pound (9-10 crackers); problems of hardness, wet, mold, maggots and weevils; the 'Hard Crackers, Come Again No More' parody; information drawn from Billings, Hardtack and Coffee.
sources.notes: Page last updated 2016. Hardtack details are credited to Billings (1887) rather than to archival records. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: Molds on Food: Are They Dangerous?
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: Some molds produce mycotoxins; mold roots can run deep and invisible bacteria can grow with it; molds tolerate salt and sugar better than most invaders; handling table says to discard moldy bread and baked goods because porous foods can be contaminated below the surface; do not sniff moldy food.
sources.notes: Page last updated 2013. It does not discuss ship's biscuit or hardtack; the application to dry hard bread is our reading and is labelled editor's note. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (full text)
sources.publisher: Randolph B. Marcy; Harper & Brothers, New York (Internet Archive text of the Library of Congress copy)
sources.supports: Chapter I 'Stores and Provisions': packing of bacon, pork and flour; Marcy's allowance for a grown person for 110 days (flour or its equivalent in hard bread, bacon or pork, coffee, sugar, with beef on the hoof); desiccated vegetables; antiscorbutics; 'cold flour'; his description of pemmican as the near-sole diet of the Fur Company's men; Dr Rae's 1854 daily allowance; the 1857-58 winter ration failure; the 'Jerking Meat' section.
sources.notes: OCR text of the same scan (identifier prairietravelerh01marc) that the Library of Congress catalogues; OCR is noisy and quotations were checked against two readings. The LOC copy is dated 1861 (Harper, 'new edition'); the book was first published in 1859. We quote only a few words. Extent read: from the OCR of the whole book (about 535,000 characters) I read the contents list, Chapter I "Stores and Provisions" (book pp. 29-36) and the "Jerking Meat" section (pp. 160-161). The rest of the 381-page book was not read.

sources.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (Library of Congress digitized book)
sources.publisher: Library of Congress (Joseph Meredith Toner Collection); Randolph B. Marcy, Harper & Brothers, 1861
sources.supports: Catalogue and contents: 'published by authority of the War Department'; Chapter I contents list 'Stores and Provisions ... Pemmican ... Antiscorbutics ... Cold Flour'; Chapter V includes 'Jerking Meat'; rights statement says the book is in the public domain.
sources.notes: The LOC page-level text view did not load for us; the passages we quote were read in the Internet Archive text of the same scan (see hist-food-marcy-prairie-traveler-text). Extent read: the item landing page (catalogue record, contents list and a few page-level OCR excerpts); the page-level text view did not load.

sources.title: Trails to Utah and the Pacific diaries and letters, 1846-1869
sources.publisher: Library of Congress (American Memory-derived collection; source material from Brigham Young University and Utah Academic Libraries Consortium)
sources.supports: The collection comprises 49 diaries, 43 maps, 82 photographs and illustrations and seven published guides for emigrants, covering Mormon and other pioneers moving to Utah, Montana and the Pacific between 1847 and 1869.
sources.notes: Only the collection-level description was read. We did not open individual diaries, so no diary text is quoted or paraphrased from it. The placeholder titled this 'Pioneer diaries collection'; this is the actual title. Extent read: the collection-level description only. No individual diary was opened.

sources.title: Historical Origins of Food Preservation
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation, University of Georgia (Brian A. Nummer, Ph.D., May 2002)
sources.supports: Overview of drying, freezing, fermenting, pickling, curing, jam and jelly, and canning; Appert's 1790s discovery and about 1806 French Navy trial; Durand's tin cans in 1810; Pasteur 1864; Chevalier-Appert's 1851 pressure retort; nitrites and C. botulinum recognised in the 1920s.
sources.notes: A 2002 overview that gives some claims without citation (for example 12,000 B.C. drying, ketchup origins). We use only the dated canning, curing and refrigeration statements, and flag the rest as undocumented. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: Jerky
sources.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation, University of Georgia (from So Easy to Preserve, 6th ed., Bulletin 989)
sources.supports: Jerky raw-meat hazards; wild game and pork trichinella treatment; heating meat strips to 160 F either in marinade before drying or in an oven after drying; fecal contamination of game; properly dried jerky keeps at room temperature two weeks in a sealed container.
sources.notes: Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id. Source of an official disagreement: NCHFP allows the 160 F heat step after drying; USDA FSIS recommends it before dehydrating and says home-dried jerky keeps 1 to 2 months. See hist-food-fsis-jerky. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

sources.title: Jerky and Food Safety
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline's current recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating; explanation that dehydrators may not reach that temperature and that bacteria become more heat resistant after drying; venison fecal contamination; home-dried jerky stored 1 to 2 months, commercially packaged 12 months.
sources.notes: Last updated November 2016. The old FSIS path .../meat/jerky-and-food-safety now returns 404. Extent read: the page via verbatim extraction (recommendation, reasoning, wild game and storage passages, update date) plus a search excerpt of the same page; ask.fsis.usda.gov repeats the 160 F / 165 F recommendation in a search excerpt only.

sources.title: Smoking Meat and Poultry
sources.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.supports: FSIS defines smoking as slowly cooking food indirectly over a fire and gives modern guidance for hot smoking in a purpose-built smoker: approved materials, no makeshift galvanized containers, thermometer monitoring and cooking to safe minimum internal temperatures.
sources.notes: This page covers hot smoking as cooking. It does not cover cold smoking or traditional smoke-curing, and we say so on the page. Extent read: verbatim extraction of the definition, makeshift-container warning, temperature range, timing and update date, plus a search excerpt of the page. Cold smoking and curing are not mentioned in the text we saw.

sources.title: Pemmican
sources.publisher: The Canadian Encyclopedia (John E. Foster; updated by Daniel Baird)
sources.supports: Definition (dried meat, traditionally bison, with fat, sometimes berries; Cree pimikan, 'manufactured grease'); bison-hide bags and shipping to provision voyageurs; Peter Pond credited with introducing pemmican to the trade in 1779 after obtaining it from the Chipewyans in the Athabasca region; posts on the Red, Assiniboine and North Saskatchewan Rivers acquired pemmican from Aboriginal peoples and the Metis; the 1814 Pemmican Proclamation of Governor Miles Macdonell; the Royal Navy later provisioning Arctic expeditions with beef pemmican made in England.
sources.notes: Gives a proportion for the ingredients that we deliberately omit. The article's etymology (pimikan, 'manufactured grease') differs from the Metis museum document's gloss; see cluster notes. Extent read: the article text through the History section via verbatim extraction. The page has a "Recipe" section that was not read and nothing was drawn from it.

sources.title: The Hudson's Bay Company Trading System (The Metis Fur Trade)
sources.publisher: Virtual Museum of Metis History and Culture (metismuseum.ca); authors Patrick Young, Todd Paquin and Darren Prefontaine
sources.supports: The HBC's constant need for provisions gave Metis bison hunters and pemmican provisioners their only steady market; Metis writer Alexander Ross's account of a hunt in which over 2500 animals were killed yielding 375 bags of pemmican and 240 bales of dried meat; provisioning was lucrative; pemmican prices rose sharply by the mid-1870s as few Metis lived off the hunt.
sources.notes: A 42-page PDF; our extraction read only some passages, so claims are limited to those. The publisher of the virtual museum (believed to be the Gabriel Dumont Institute) was not confirmed from a page we read and is not asserted. A search excerpt of this document gives the Cree gloss 'pimmi' (fat) and 'konn' (meat); we did not confirm that wording in the PDF text. Extent read: a 42-page PDF of which only a few passages (the HBC provisioning and Ross hunt paragraphs and the title/authors) were returned by verbatim extraction, roughly one page of text in total. The rest was not read.

sources.title: About The Jump! (Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump)
sources.publisher: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump World Heritage Site, Alberta, Canada
sources.supports: The site's account that the Blackfoot (Siksika, Kainai/Bloods and Piikani/Peigan) pursued traditional lifeways until the buffalo's near extinction in 1881; that in fall communal kills occurred and 'the people would prepare dry meat and pemmican for winter', held as emergency supplies; Treaty No. Seven (1877).
sources.notes: The site's operator and its Blackfoot partnership are not stated on the page we read; we attribute the words to the site, not to named Blackfoot authors. Extent read: the page text via verbatim extraction (history of the site, tribes, seasonal travel, Treaty 7). The linked booklet "Buffalo Tracks" was not read.

sources.title: Lesson 9: How to Make Wasna
sources.publisher: NATIFS (North American Traditional Indigenous Food Systems)
sources.supports: NATIFS's statement that the food is known as wasna to the Lakota and Dakota people and as pemmican to Anishinaabe peoples, that Indigenous peoples across the Plains and beyond have long relied on it for hunts, seasonal travel and winter, and that many still make and share it today.
sources.notes: The organisation's homepage states a mission to promote Indigenous foodways education and food access and names Chef Sean Sherman as executive director. The lesson contains a method; we neither quote nor link the method. Kind 'nonprofit' is the closest fit (nonprofit status not confirmed from the pages read). Extent read: the lesson's introductory cultural-context paragraphs only, via verbatim extraction. The method section was deliberately not read into this archive. The organisation's About page returned 404; its homepage was seen only as a search excerpt.

sources.title: InterTribal Buffalo Council (Northern Plains History and Cultures)
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Native Knowledge 360
sources.supports: The bison was more than a historical food source to Northern Plains Native Nations; tribal histories, cultures, traditions and spiritual lives were connected to the buffalo in a reciprocal relationship, and people honored and cared for the bison through ceremonies and cultural protocols.
sources.notes: A classroom resource for grades 9-12. Extent read: the opening paragraph only (verbatim extraction). The rest of the lesson was not read.

sources.title: Preservation of Meat
sources.publisher: Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation), Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia
sources.supports: Enslaved workers Ursula Granger and John cut meat for hams, bacon and salt pork, covered it in salt to draw out moisture, and hung it in the smokehouse over a low-burning hardwood fire; the preserved pork, beef, mutton and fish was rationed to enslaved people, hired workers and Jefferson's household; prime cuts went to the household and less desirable cuts to enslaved workers.
sources.notes: A short entry. It gives no quantities, times or temperatures, and we found none elsewhere in our sources. Extent read: full entry text (a short paragraph and a caption), live scrape.

sources.title: Smokehouse
sources.publisher: George Washington's Mount Vernon
sources.supports: The smokehouse (built 1775, per the site's virtual tour) smoked bacon and ham over a fire pit; enslaved workers salted or pickled the meat and hung it over a smoldering fire; for storage the meats stayed hanging or were packed in barrels of ashes; the building was locked during curing to prevent theft, and the farm manager's 1795 letter reports bacon stolen; Washington could smoke upwards of 300 hams a year.
sources.notes: Gives no curing quantities or temperatures. The restoration was sponsored by a commercial ham producer, as the page itself states. Extent read: full page text including "About the Smokehouse" and the virtual-tour caption, live scrape.

sources.title: Keeping your (food) cool: From ice harvesting to electric refrigeration
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.supports: Underground cold stores and icehouses; natural ice harvesting taking off in the early 1800s with Frederic Tudor; wooden iceboxes lined with tin or zinc by the end of the 1800s; the museum's view that cold became the clear choice because salting, drying and canning erased any appearance of freshness and took longer to prepare; electric refrigeration (1914 DOMELRE; General Electric Monitor top in 1927).
sources.notes: Read through a search result that reproduced the full page text; flagged for a human link check. Extent read: the full article text as reproduced in a search-result excerpt; the live page was not separately scraped.

sources.title: The Icebox, the Predecessor of Modern Refrigeration
sources.publisher: National Park Service
sources.supports: How an icebox worked; ice cut from ponds in winter and stored in insulated ice houses; Frederic Tudor shipped ice widely; in 1847 nearly 52,000 tons of ice moved by ship or train to 28 US cities; ice-making factories replaced harvesting; the first widely popular electric refrigerator was General Electric's in 1927; 85% of American households had a refrigerator by 1944.
sources.notes: Read through a search result that reproduced the full page text; flagged for a human link check. Extent read: the full page text as reproduced in a search-result excerpt; the live page was not separately scraped.

sources.title: Traveling the Emigrant Trails
sources.publisher: National Park Service (National Historic Trails)
sources.supports: Cost of an 1850 outfit; the supply list from Joseph Ware's 1849 Emigrant's Guide for three people on the Oregon Trail (flour 1,080 lb, bacon 600 lb, coffee 100 lb, sugar 150 lb, and so on, plus hard-tack, dried beef, molasses, vinegar, beans); food emigrants carried and the game they hunted; buffalo chips as fuel; snakes or prairie dogs 'in desperate times'.
sources.notes: Read in query mode (verbatim extraction). Does not say how the guide's quantities relate to Marcy's per-person figures; see cluster notes. Extent read: the Supplies and Food on the Trail sections in full via verbatim extraction, plus the update date. Other sections were not read.

sources.title: National Historic Trails Auto Tour Route Interpretive Guide: Nevada
sources.publisher: National Park Service (National Trails Intermountain Region; April 2012, fourth printing June 2021)
sources.supports: The Bidwell-Bartleson party's provisions gone by autumn 1841 and the butchering of oxen; Dawson's remark about packing provisions; on the Humboldt in the main emigration years nobody discarded bacon, flour or beans and many parties were dangerously low; the 1846 Donner-Reed party realizing they lacked food; Hastings Cutoff passing Salt Lake City where travelers could buy provisions after 1847; the NPS account of Western Shoshone (Newe) and Paiute (Numa) hunger, loss of pine nut groves and seed grasses, and livestock raids; quoted emigrant and observer statements (Bidwell, Greeley, Shaw, Langworthy).
sources.notes: A 104-page PDF; our extraction returned the passages above in full and we rely only on them. The Shoshone account of the emigrants is the guide's retelling of an oral tradition and is attributed that way. Extent read: a 104-page PDF. Verbatim extraction returned a long run of narrative (Bidwell-Bartleson, Humboldt, Donner-Reed and 'Politics of Hunger' passages, perhaps 20 pages' worth). Pages not returned were not read.
